title: Executable rules: Formalisation conceals interpretive choices
desc: Contrasts computational demonstrations with legal understanding and converges on narrow, expert-informed, explainable support.

kps.k: The central dispute concerns whether executable legal rules capture expertise or provide only a bounded aid to legal work.
kps.d: The historical account in Is Law Computable? traces early confidence to an analogy with medical expert systems and an assumption that law would prove easier to formalise. The British Nationality Act authors claim feasibility for implementing rules and regulations, while Susskind envisages specialised practitioner assistance. Leith’s retrospective critique challenges the stronger ambition of encapsulating lawyers’ knowledge and tactical judgment. These positions distinguish useful computation from a complete model of legal reasoning; they do not establish the capabilities of contemporary generative AI.

kps.k: Formalisation can conceal interpretive choices even when it successfully executes rules.
kps.d: Leith argues that static representations miss how context and narratives constructed from interpreted facts continually shape legal meaning. Susskind identifies fact classification as a crucial non-deductive step that contemporary systems did not support. Stepping Stones adds that programmers can make law appear more consistent and complete by removing ambiguity, conflict and gaps. Yet it also reports that modelling the British Nationality Act exposed undefined predicates and loopholes: formalisation can reveal legal problems as well as obscure them.

qs.q: I do not mean that law changes gradually over time - it certainly does that - but it also depends largely upon the context in which it is used and how it is used to produce a narrative from the interpreted facts of a situation (and this evidences continual micro-changes, both developmental and revisionary).
qs.a: The Rise and Fall of the Legal Expert System · Academia · 2010

qs.q: Perhaps the most telling objection to deduction in law with regard to all the projects is what can be termed The Argument from Particularity of Facts.73 This asserts that the crucial, and non- deductive, stage in legal reasoning is that of classifying the particular facts of the case, a stage in which none of the current computer systems are of support.
qs.a: Expert Systems in Law: A Jurisprudential Approach to Artificial Intelligence and Legal Reasoning · Academia · 1986

kps.k: The methodological disagreement concerns how legal understanding should guide computational design, not simply whether to use logic.
kps.d: Susskind argues that jurisprudence should supply models before implementation, while acknowledging disagreement among legal theories. The British Nationality Act authors distinguish logical representation from Prolog execution and describe a practical, top-down method that deferred difficult knowledge-representation questions until requirements emerged. Leith disputes the approach’s logical justification and treatment of social context. The reviewer of Susskind’s book accepts concerns about engineers’ legal knowledge but rejects Leith’s interpretation of their objectives, treating Susskind’s account as compatible with the logic programmers’ conclusions.

kps.k: Technical demonstrations and application examples do not settle the dispute over operational success.
kps.d: In 1986, Susskind judged limited-scope construction technically feasible but reported no fully operational system useful to the profession; Waterman and Peterson’s LDS still required substantial refinement. The British Nationality Act excerpts offer feasibility claims, not quantitative accuracy or deployment results. Stepping Stones credits the separate Latent Damage System with usefulness and cites administrative applications. Leith later questions laboratory-to-workplace success and independent testing, drawing partly on a 1988 assessment of expert systems generally. The evidence therefore differs in date, scope and outcome measured rather than forming a single comparable test of success.

kps.k: The practical convergence favours narrow, expert-informed support with substantive explanations and demonstrated user value.
kps.d: Susskind recommends intensive coverage of specialised domains, expert-derived heuristics, explanations grounded in legal authorities and access to primary sources. Encoding statutes alone does not meet his standard of expertise. Leith likewise urges developers to solve lawyers’ working problems, although he questions market demand and identifies liability as a partial obstacle to public-facing advice systems. The reviewer advocates domain-led research and tentatively proposes interdisciplinary education. These recommendations support practitioner assistance without requiring acceptance of claims that systems can preserve expertise indefinitely or outperform individual experts.

qs.q: It is not clear that there ever was - there was certainly an early belief that nonexperts would be able to utilise systems which gave them legal advice, for example, but that quickly evaporated - partly due to liability issues which scared off selling legal and other advisory systems to the public.
qs.a: The Rise and Fall of the Legal Expert System · Academia · 2010

kps.k: Predictions about growth and explanations of failure remain distinct from demonstrated outcomes.
kps.d: Stepping Stones predicts proliferation because inexpensive tools could address strained expert resources, without claiming a complete model of legal argument. Susskind presents preservation and wider distribution of expertise as possibilities within a decades-long research agenda. Leith instead attributes inflated expectations and neglected alternatives to funding incentives, particularly Alvey support, but explicitly speculates about how search and citation tools might otherwise have developed. The resulting practical implication is to test demand, utility and limitations rather than infer success from technical promise or failure from a speculative alternative history.

qs.q: There are abundant examples of applica- tions, many motivated by a need for practical, labor-saving tools in the trenches, where expert resources are terribly strained.4 8 Given the availa- bility of inexpensive expert systems development tools and rule-based pro- gramming languages, such application systems will continue to proliferate;

vlens.an:
The curated academia-and-research sources broadly accept the proposition that executable legal rules are bounded aids rather than complete representations of legal expertise, and several materially develop its preferred design approach. Common reasons include the interpretive work hidden by formalisation, especially resolving ambiguity and classifying facts; the contextual and dynamic character of legal meaning; weak evidence that technical demonstrations became operationally useful systems; and the need for narrow applications informed by legal experts and capable of substantive explanation. Their principal extension is methodological: jurisprudence should shape computational models, domain experts should define appropriate questions and assessment criteria, and logical representation should be distinguished from its implementation in a particular language.

There is material internal variation. The British Nationality Act authors are comparatively optimistic about feasibility and treat top-down formalisation as a practical experiment, while acknowledging that difficult knowledge-representation and commonsense issues were deferred; they provide no quantitative deployment evidence. Susskind and the jurisprudential reviewer retain confidence in specialised practitioner assistance but require expert-derived knowledge, legal-theoretical grounding and explanations tied to authority. Stepping Stones similarly regards rule-based systems as useful for narrow applications while explicitly denying that they form a complete model of legal argument. Leith is more sceptical, stressing lost social context, inadequate validation and uncertain user demand, yet converges on support for tools addressing lawyers’ actual work. The introductory historical account alone remains noncommittal because it reports early confidence without evaluating the cluster’s preferred model. These differences concern the degree of confidence in formalisation and the best development method, not an overall rejection of bounded, expert-informed support.

qs.q: Knowledge domains always look more straightforwardly translateable into rules when viewed from the outside: domain experts both find they cannot fully express their knowledge in the form of rules, and resist the attempts of outsiders to do so as misconceived.
qs.a: Review of Richard Susskind, Expert Systems in Law — A Jurisprudential Inquiry (OUP 1987) · Academia · 1989

qs.q: Demonstrations are now in the context, and according to the criteria, of the knowledge domain, rather than the technology.

elens.an: The pre-2015 sources support the proposition that executable legal rules can be useful in bounded settings but do not, by themselves, capture legal expertise or eliminate interpretation. Common reasons are that encoding resolves or suppresses ambiguity, factual classification and contextual judgment remain outside straightforward deduction, and technical feasibility is distinct from demonstrated professional utility. They also converge on narrow, expert-informed systems assessed by legal-domain criteria and capable of substantive explanation. Material variation concerns degree and method rather than the proposition’s core: the British Nationality Act authors are comparatively optimistic about formalisation’s feasibility and use a pragmatic top-down method; Susskind supports specialised practitioner assistance grounded in jurisprudence; the review strengthens the case for domain-led design while defending logic-programming research from some criticism; and Leith offers the strongest retrospective challenge, emphasising law’s dynamic context, weak validation and neglected user needs. These curated sources therefore should not be treated as representative of all pre-2015 scholarship, and their application examples and predictions do not amount to comparable evidence of operational success.

elens.an: The source retrospectively documents the early confidence behind legal expert systems: proponents inferred from applications in medicine that legal rules could be formalised and used to generate advice. Its framing distinguishes those historical assumptions from demonstrated capability, which is compatible with the synthesis’s caution about equating executable rules with legal expertise. However, it does not directly argue that formalisation conceals interpretive choices, assess operational outcomes, or endorse narrow, expert-informed and explainable support. Because this time-period facet contains only one curated source, there is no basis for identifying a shared view across sources; the material variation is instead between the optimism being reported and the retrospective author’s distancing from it.
